opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first instinct with a loss spike is not to panic. A spike by itself doesn't tell you much. What matters is what happens next. If the loss shoots up and comes back down within a few hundred steps, and the downstream evals don't show lasting damage, often the most sensible thing is to let it ride. Overreacting can cost you more compute and time than the spike ever would.

That said, you can't ignore them either, because spikes are often symptoms. So the first thing I'd want to know is *why* it happened. In practice there are a few usual suspects. One is data: a batch with weird, repetitive, or corrupted content, extremely long sequences, or some domain the model hasn't seen much of. Another is optimization: the learning rate being slightly too aggressive at that scale, Adam's second-moment estimates getting stale so the effective update suddenly blows up, or attention logits and certain activations growing until something numerically tips over. And sometimes it's plain infrastructure, like a bad node, a precision issue, or a communication bug.

For the short-term fix, the common playbook is to roll back to a checkpoint before the spike, skip or reshuffle the offending data batches, and maybe lower the learning rate a bit for a while before ramping back up. That works surprisingly often. But if you keep having to do it, it means the recipe itself is fragile, and the rollback is just a band-aid.

So the more important work, in my view, is prevention through design: better initialization, normalization choices like QK-norm, careful gradient clipping, tuning Adam's epsilon and betas, monitoring things like max attention logits and per-layer gradient norms so you see trouble coming before the loss does, and doing serious validation on small-scale runs so you understand how stability changes as you scale up. Data cleaning and deduplication matter a lot here too.

The bigger philosophy is that at large scale, every restart is extremely expensive, so stability isn't a nice-to-have, it's part of the efficiency story. A team that understands its training dynamics well can be bold on things like learning rate and throughput because it trusts the run won't fall apart. So I'd say: handle individual spikes pragmatically, but treat a pattern of spikes as a research problem worth solving properly.

r001.rationale: The response recommends letting a brief spike pass and suggests rollback, skipping batches, or lowering the learning rate. It does not recommend halting training to resolve the spike.

fable-5.1.text:
Loss spikes are one of those things that look scary on the dashboard but, in my experience, you shouldn't panic about them. The first question I always ask is whether the spike is actually temporary. If the loss jumps and then comes back down to the original trend within a few hundred steps, that's usually fine. The model is probably hitting a batch of unusual data, or the optimizer state got briefly out of sync with the gradient landscape. You watch it, you don't intervene.

The dangerous case is when the spike doesn't recover, or when it recovers to a plateau that's higher than before. That tells you something structural went wrong, often in the attention logits or in layer norms where activations are blowing up. At that point you can't just wait it out.

The practical playbook most teams converge on is pretty simple. You checkpoint frequently, so when a spike turns out to be real, you can roll back a few thousand steps instead of losing days. Then you skip the batch that caused it, or shuffle the data order, and often that alone is enough. If it keeps recurring, you look at the learning rate schedule, because a lot of spikes are really a sign that the learning rate is too aggressive for that stage of training. Lowering it slightly or adding warmup after the restart usually stabilizes things.

Beyond that, there are architectural choices that make the whole process less fragile in the first place. Things like QK normalization, careful initialization, and gradient clipping that's tuned rather than just set to a default value. If you've done this well, you'll still see spikes, but they'll almost always be the harmless kind.

So my honest answer is: don't treat every spike as an emergency, but build your infrastructure so that when one is an emergency, recovering from it costs you hours rather than weeks. The teams that struggle with this usually aren't struggling because of the spikes themselves. They're struggling because they didn't plan for them.

r001.rationale: The response says to watch a spike that recovers within a few hundred steps and not intervene. It recommends action only when the spike fails to recover or leaves a higher plateau, so it does not recommend halting training to resolve temporary spikes.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t treat every temporary loss spike as a reason to stop training. First, I’d check whether the loss recovers and whether the spike shows up elsewhere—in gradient norms, for example, or in validation performance. An unusual batch can produce a spike without indicating a broader problem.

If it recovers quickly, I’d keep monitoring rather than immediately change the training setup. If the spikes persist or become more frequent, I’d investigate the data, numerical stability, and learning rate. The key is to distinguish a brief fluctuation from an instability that’s actually getting worse.

r001.rationale: The response advises against stopping for every temporary spike and recommends monitoring or investigating persistent spikes; it does not recommend halting training to resolve them.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t stop a training run just because of a brief loss spike. I’d first check whether the loss recovers and whether gradient norms, numerical stability, and validation performance look healthy. A spike can come from an unusual batch, so it’s useful to inspect the data around that step before changing anything.

If the spikes persist or the model stops recovering, then I’d investigate the learning rate, optimizer state, and data quality. Depending on the cause, I might lower the learning rate, adjust gradient clipping, or resume from a healthy checkpoint. The key is to distinguish a temporary fluctuation from sustained instability.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would not stop training for a brief loss spike and recommends monitoring recovery and stability instead.
